findings.title: Adding abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider SPI implementations
findings.body: The new `int order()` method was added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface as an abstract (non-default) method. Any third-party or downstream implementation of this SPI (custom crypto providers, adapters, older keycloak-client jars on the same classpath) will no longer compile and, if precompiled, will fail at runtime with an AbstractMethodError when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` on them. Since this is a public extension interface, the new method should have a default implementation (e.g., `default int order() { return 0; }`) to preserve binary compatibility.

findings.title: Equal order() values across DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider make provider selection nondeterministic
findings.body: DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider previously threw an IllegalStateException when multiple providers were found; now it silently picks the first after sorting, but the sort is stable only relative to ServiceLoader iteration order, which depends on classpath ordering. In a deployment that (accidentally or intentionally) has more than one of these providers on the classpath, e.g. a FIPS environment where keycloak-crypto-fips1402 and keycloak-crypto-default are both present, the non-FIPS provider may win arbitrarily, silently disabling FIPS mode. Either the FIPS provider should have a strictly higher order, or ties among full-featured providers should still be reported as an error.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider (e.g. SUN), not a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a stock JVM is the SUN provider, not BouncyCastle. Callers of this method (e.g. code in keycloak-common that fetches the provider to register it or relies on it being BC/BCFIPS, or that checks `getBouncyCastleProvider().getName()`) will silently get a provider that does not implement the BC algorithms they expect, leading to hard-to-diagnose NoSuchAlgorithmException failures. At minimum this is misleading for the interface contract documented as 'BouncyCastle security provider'; if BC is not available, throwing UnsupportedOperationException (as done for the other methods) would fail fast and predictably.

findings.title: Most CryptoProvider operations throw UnsupportedOperationException, breaking authz-client features beyond ECDSA signature conversion
findings.body: The provider registered via META-INF/services in the authz-client jar throws UnsupportedOperationException for getPemUtils(), getCertificateUtils(), getX509CertFactory(), getKeyFactory(), getSignature(), getAlgorithmProvider() etc. CryptoIntegration.init is now called from AuthzClient.create, so if this is the only provider discoverable via the AuthzClient classloader, any code path in keycloak-common/authz-client that touches those APIs will fail at runtime — for example parsing PEM keys/certificates for client JWT assertion signing, or JWKS handling. Previously, these paths worked whenever BC was on the classpath via DefaultCryptoProvider; now a working deployment can regress to UnsupportedOperationException. Each unsupported method should either be implemented with JCE defaults (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or the design should ensure DefaultCryptoProvider is used when available.

findings.title: Dead code: two ASN1Encoder instances created and written to, then discarded
findings.body: In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, lines 114–115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write the r and s BigIntegers into them, and throw the results away; the actual encoding happens in the following statement. This is leftover debug/dead code that wastes work and confuses readers; it should be removed.

findings.title: Indefinite-length DER (0x80) is returned as -1 and causes NegativeArraySizeException instead of a clean error
findings.body: readLength() maps the indefinite-length marker 0x80 to -1. In readSequence(), a length of -1 makes the `while (length > 0)` loop simply skip parsing and return an empty list (silently accepting malformed input), and in readNext() the -1 propagates to read(-1), where `new byte[-1]` throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException rather than an IOException. Since BER indefinite-length encodings are not valid DER for ECDSA signatures, they should be rejected with an explicit IOException.

findings.title: Test uses one default-curve key pair for all algorithms and only checks round-trip, not interop with the BC implementation
findings.body: The test generates a single key pair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") without specifying a curve, so ES384/ES512 cases run with (typically) a P-256 key and only exercise zero-padding logic, never real 48/66-byte coordinates. More importantly, it only verifies that this provider's conversion round-trips with itself; it does not compare output against DefaultCryptoProvider/BouncyCastle (e.g., BCECDSACryptoProvider) to guarantee signature compatibility with what the Keycloak server produces/expects. A cross-check against the BC implementation per curve would catch subtle encoding mismatches (leading-zero handling, negative integers) that a self-round-trip cannot.
